maestro plugin

Usage: maestro plugin <command> [options]

Commands:
  create             Scaffold a new Maestro plugin from a template
  types              Write the TypeScript typings for Maestro plugins into a plugin folder
  test               Run a plugin's own tests on this machine, unsandboxed: only for code you trust
  check              Validate a plugin, render each components panel once on this machine (unsandboxed: only for code you trust), and statically check each custom editor
  validate           Check a plugin folder, manifest or catalog the way Maestro will load it
  inspect            Show what a plugin folder contributes, the access it asks for, and its content hash
  release-entry      Print the catalog release entry for a plugin folder's committed HEAD
  list               List plugins on the Maestro host with their status and access level
  logs               Print the recent log lines of a plugin
  enable             Enable a plugin; code and capabilities need --approve
  disable            Disable a plugin
  system on          Turn plugins on for the Maestro host
  system off         Turn plugins off for the Maestro host
  restart            Stop a plugin's worker so its next command or event starts it fresh
  dev watch          Load a plugin folder, then stream its logs and reloads until Ctrl-C
  dev load           Load a plugin folder into Maestro as a development plugin
  dev reload         Reload development plugins now, or one folder and re-check its approval
  dev inspect        Open DevTools for a plugin's open panels and editors
  dev emit           Fire a test event at a development plugin's worker and open panels
  dev hook           Run a hook through a development plugin's worker and print what the chain decided
  dev request        Call a development plugin's worker handler the way a panel's plugin.request does
  dev unload         Remove a development folder from Maestro

Usage: maestro plugin install <publisher.id|owner/repo[@ref]|git-url|page-url|dir> [--ref <ref>] [--catalog <official|community|id|url>] [--approve <fingerprint>] [--json]

Options:

  --pairing-code <code>  Run against a remote Maestro server using an orca://pair?... code

Notes:
  Sources: a catalog id (publisher.id), owner/repo[@ref] on GitHub, any https:// or ssh:// Git URL or git@host:owner/repo.git, a GitHub or GitLab release, tag or tree page URL, or a folder path. Without a version Maestro installs the newest version tag (vX.Y.Z), else the default branch, always pinned to the exact commit.
  Git runs on the Maestro host with that host's own credentials (credential helper such as `gh auth setup-git`, Git Credential Manager or osxkeychain, or the SSH agent) and never prompts. A repository it cannot read fails with git_auth_failed, which names the host and how to sign Git in there. URLs carrying a username or token are refused.

Anything that runs code or acts in Maestro fails with approval_required before anything is written; it lists what it would be granted, why, the publisher and repository, and the exact command to re-run with --approve <fingerprint>, which is bound to that plugin, version, files and access.

maestro plugin test

Usage: maestro plugin test [dir] [--json]

Run a plugin's own tests on this machine, unsandboxed: only for code you trust

Options:
  --help                 Show this help message
  --json                 Emit machine-readable JSON
  --dir

Notes:
  Not sandboxed: this runs the plugin's code and tests on this machine with your user's full access, outside Maestro's plugin sandbox. Run it only on code you trust.
  Runs every *.test.ts(x) (also .mts, .js, .jsx, .mjs) under the folder, skipping node_modules, .orca, dist and dot-folders. The folder defaults to the current one.
  Uses Node's built-in test runner (node:test), or the plugin's own vitest when it has one in node_modules. No config: `orca` and `orca/testing` resolve to the files this Maestro ships, and sources are transpiled and imported exactly as Maestro loads them.
  Runs on the `node` on PATH when it is 20.6 or newer, else on the Node built into Maestro, so no Node install is needed. It does not reach the Maestro app.
  Exit code: the runner's (0 when every test passes). With --json the runner output goes to stderr and one result object to stdout.

Examples:
  $ maestro plugin test .
  $ maestro plugin test ./todo-panel --json

maestro serve service install

Usage: maestro serve service install [--port <port>] [--bind <ip>] [--pairing-address <host>] [--allow-public | --refuse-public] [--command <path>] [--dry-run] [--json]

Run maestro serve as a per-user background service that restarts itself

Options:
  --help                 Show this help message
  --json                 Emit machine-readable JSON
  --port
  --bind
  --pairing-address
  --allow-public
  --refuse-public
  --command <text>       Command to run in the terminal on startup
  --dry-run

Notes:
  macOS writes a LaunchAgent; Linux writes a systemd user unit. Both run `maestro serve --supervise --no-pairing` for this profile, so the server restarts with growing delays and gives up after repeated failures instead of looping.
  The service never prints a pairing link to its log. Pair clients with `maestro pair` while it runs, or from the desktop app.
  On Linux the service stops at logout unless lingering is on (`loginctl enable-linger`); install reports it.
  Reinstalling replaces the unit and clears a previous give-up. --command defaults to the installed Maestro app's `maestro` command on PATH (`maestro` on Linux) and must not be a launcher tied to one Maestro version. --dry-run prints the unit without installing it.
  Needs the Maestro app installed on this machine. The `maestro` command in an Maestro terminal on an SSH host belongs to that connection's server and cannot install a service.
  Not available on Windows yet.

Examples:
  $ maestro serve service install
  $ maestro serve service install --port 6768 --bind 127.0.0.1 --dry-run
